strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a real regime (BO with many observations, 'BOMO') where GP hyperparameter fitting is the bottleneck, and carefully distinguishes it from high-dimensional BO.

ENN is a simple, well-executed surrogate: precision-weighted KNN with distance-based epistemic variance, achieving genuinely O(N) fitting and acquisition, with a clever fitting-free variant (NDS over (mu, sigma)) for noise-free problems.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five realistic simulation/HPO tasks, both natural and frozen noise protocols, 30 repetitions, and a thoughtful baseline set including TuRBO, Optuna, CMA-ES, a random baseline, and a surrogate-free ablation (turbo-zero) that probes whether the surrogate is actually needed.

Scaling claims are directly supported: Figure 1 shows the O(N^2) vs O(N) scaling separation against GP, sparse GP, Vecchia, and Parzen-estimator baselines, and Table 1 reports proposal times up to N=50,000 with speedups of 10-150x.

Honest limitations section (fixed K, no ARD, Euclidean distance degradation with D, no Thompson sampling support, no regret bounds), and the authors candidly note that CMA-ES is O(1) and performs very well, which strengthens credibility.
Released, pip-installable implementation with source and examples supports reproducibility.

Appendix A provides a genuine theoretical contribution: proofs of local consistency, sequential no-empty-ball, and improvement properties connecting ENN to the PseudoBO convergence framework of Chen & Lam (2025).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: ENN is essentially inverse-square-distance-weighted KNN regression with a heuristic variance, closely related to nearest-neighbor GP methods (Gramacy & Apley 2015; Wu et al. 2024) that the paper itself cites; the contribution is more an engineering simplification than a new idea.

The convergence guarantee is overstated relative to what is proven: Appendix A proves the IP property for a scalarized acquisition lambda*mu + (1-lambda)*sigma, and Remark 2 concedes the actual implemented acquisition (uniform sampling from the first Pareto front of NDS) is only 'closely related'. Additionally, the PBO framework is verified for the noise-free variant only, and it is unclear that TuRBO's trust-region restriction and restarts satisfy Chen & Lam's standing regularity conditions (acquisition over a shrinking trust region is not acquisition over the full domain).

The solution-quality claim of 'comparable' is only loosely supported: in several natural-noise plots turbo-enn visibly lags turbo-one (e.g., LunarLander-v3, Hopper-v5), and there is no statistical analysis of quality differences, only mean +/- two standard errors read off plots.

The core value proposition is undermined by the authors' own baselines: turbo-zero (surrogate-free RAASP sampling) and CMA-ES are often competitive on frozen-noise tasks, raising the question of whether the surrogate is earning its complexity in the regimes where the method is fastest.
Fixed K=10 and beta=1 with no sensitivity analysis; the noisy variant has no theoretical treatment, and the uncertainty estimates are never evaluated for calibration quality.

No comparison to other scalable surrogates for large N (neural-network or random-forest surrogates are excluded by fiat), so the empirical claim of being the practical choice in this regime rests on a partial baseline set.

Presentation is uneven: notation glitches (log[L(theta)), typos ('onces', 'simulation optimization problems'), inconsistent naming (turbo-zero/turbo-0), and the header claim of 'up to 50,000 observations' rests mainly on one task (Hopper-v5 frozen) while the controlled scaling study in Figure 1 only reaches N ~ 1000.
All distances are Euclidean with a single global metric; the acknowledged lack of ARD makes applicability to genuinely high-D problems (beyond LASSO-DNA at D=180) speculative.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely relevant problem (proposal-time scaling in BOMO) and clearly motivates why hyperparameter fitting of GPs, rather than acquisition-time scaling alone, is the bottleneck.
The method is simple, clearly specified, and fully reproducible: hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and an anonymized pip-installable implementation with source are provided.

Experiments are broad and reasonably rigorous: 5 simulation benchmarks plus a synthetic scaling study (Figure 1), natural vs. frozen noise protocols distinguished carefully, 30 repeats with standard errors, passive-evaluation protocol for noisy objectives, and an ablation (turbo-zero).
The observed speedups (12x to 150x in Table 1) with up to N=50,000 observations empirically support the O(N) claim, and the paper honestly acknowledges that CMA-ES is O(1) and performs well.

Limitations are discussed openly and at length (fixed K, no ARD/anisotropic distance, no joint sampling, no regret bounds), and the limitations section does not hide the competitiveness of surrogate-free baselines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: ENN is essentially inverse-squared-distance-weighted KNN regression (a decades-old estimator) with the trivial uncertainty sigma(x) = 1/sqrt(sum 1/r_i^2). The paper presents this as a 'novel surrogate,' but the mathematical content is thin, and the relationship to local GP approximations (Gramacy & Apley, 2015) and Vecchia/NNGP methods is downplayed despite being acknowledged.

The stated significance is undercut by the paper's own results. The surrogate-free baselines (cma, turbo-zero) are competitive on several benchmarks (and 'perform very well' on frozen-noise tasks per the authors' own admission), raising the question of whether a surrogate at all is needed in this regime. If CMA-ES is O(1) and comparable in solution quality, the practical value of TuRBO-ENN over much simpler methods is not convincingly established.

Theory-practice mismatch in Appendix A: the PseudoBO consistency proof applies to a scalarized acquisition alpha = lambda*mu + (1-lambda)*sigma with random lambda, but the actual algorithm samples uniformly from the first Pareto front of the NDS (Remark 2 concedes this). Moreover, the proof covers only the noise-free NDS variant, not the noisy UCB variant used in most experiments, and it does not address TuRBO's trust-region restarts/shrinking. Calling this a 'convergence guarantee' in the conclusion overstates what is proven (consistency, not regret).

The noisy-case incumbent selection (top-K by yi, then argmax mu) and the fixed K=10, beta=1, and fixed subsample size P are heuristic choices with no ablation or sensitivity analysis; the claimed 'principled uncertainty quantification' for non-GP surrogates is not validated (e.g., no calibration experiments).

Nearest-neighbor surrogates are known to degrade in high dimensions, and Euclidean distance in D=180 (LASSO-DNA) is unlikely to discriminate meaningfully; the paper acknowledges this but provides no analysis or mitigation, and the LASSO-DNA experiments use only N=1000.

Comparisons to some plausible baselines are omitted (neural/random-forest surrogates, SNoek, SMAC) with the justification of fitting complexity, while Figure 1 shows unexplained behavior for optuna (a claimed O(N) method) that is far slower than turbo-enn in Table 1 (e.g., 8995s vs. 822.8s at N=10,000), leaving fairness and implementation equivalence unclear.

Figure 1's scaling benchmark sets N = D, conflating dimension and observation count, and uses only synthetic functions; the central O(N) vs O(N^2) scaling claim would be better supported by controlled experiments isolating N.

Solution-quality gains over TuRBO are at best 'comparable' and sometimes slightly worse (e.g., LunarLander natural noise), so the contribution reduces to a speed/engineering improvement of an existing algorithm rather than a new methodological insight.

strengths: The paper targets a real and increasingly relevant problem (BOMO: BO with many observations), and clearly distinguishes it from high-dimensional BO; the motivation with concrete examples (Ax's 2D rule, Wang et al. 2016 vs Daulton et al. 2021) is well argued.

The proposed method is simple, principled enough for its purpose (precision-weighted KNN with distance-based epistemic and aleatoric variance), and the computational analysis is transparent: O(N) fitting and querying via Faiss, with careful engineering details such as subsampled LOO pseudolikelihood with fixed P and top-K incumbent selection to keep scaling linear.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation: five realistic simulation problems (Gymnasium tasks plus LASSO-DNA), up to N = 50,000 observations, 30 repetitions, mean ± 2 SE, a sensible noise-agnostic evaluation protocol (r_passive with held-out evaluation seeds), an ablation (turbo-zero) that isolates the surrogate's contribution, and baselines including Optuna, CMA-ES, Vecchia, and TuRBO variants.
Reported speedups (10-150x in proposal time) with comparable solution quality, and the scaling study in Figure 1 with 120 runs per method empirically substantiates the O(N^2) vs O(N) claim.
Good reproducibility: pip-installable library with source, explicit hyperparameter settings (K=10), and a full algorithmic description (Algorithm 1).
Honest and substantive limitations discussion (fixed K, no ARD-style metric weighting, no joint sampling so no Thompson sampling, curse of dimensionality in the distance metric, no regret bounds).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The surrogate is essentially inverse-distance-squared weighted KNN regression, a long-standing technique; the contribution is its integration into TuRBO with UCB/NDS rather than a new modeling idea. Vecchia/nnGP methods already combine nearest-neighbor conditioning with TuRBO-style trust regions, so the delta over prior art is a simplified surrogate plus engineering.

The theoretical claim is somewhat overstated relative to what is proven. Appendix A analyzes a scalarized acquisition alpha_lambda = lambda*mu + (1-lambda)*sigma, which is 'introduced solely to provide a concise, fully rigorous IP proof' (Remark 2), whereas the implemented noise-free variant samples uniformly from the NDS Pareto front. The convergence guarantee therefore technically applies to a different acquisition rule than the one evaluated. Additionally, the PBO analysis covers only the noiseless setting (LC proof assumes y_i = f(x_i), sigma -> 0 near data), so the noisy ENN+UCB variant used in the main experiments has no such guarantee.

The independence assumption over observations (each observation an independent estimate of f(x), variance c_e*d^2) is heuristic; correlated observations are the norm and the resulting uncertainty is likely miscalibrated in structured problems, but calibration is never assessed quantitatively (no coverage or calibration experiments).

On frozen-noise tasks the surrogate-free baselines (turbo-zero, CMA-ES, random) are often competitive with or better than turbo-enn, and the paper itself notes CMA-ES is O(1) and 'performs very well.' This weakens the practical significance of the surrogate replacement in a substantial portion of the experimental settings; the speedup story is most compelling for the noisy variant.

No comparison to Vecchia-based BO (VecchiaBO) in the main optimization experiments at large N, despite Figure 1 including it in the scaling study and the related-work discussion positioning ENN against it; the claimed 'significant speedup' over Vecchia is shown only for small N and never in solution-quality terms.
Fixed choices (K=10, UCB beta=1, fixed P) are not ablated; sensitivity to these choices is unknown, which matters for practitioners intending to reuse the method.

Presentation has some rough edges (e.g., 'once[s]' typo, inconsistency between turbo-zero/turbo-0 naming, pseudolikelihood notation log[L(theta) with misplaced brackets), and Figure 1 uses N = D, conflating dimension with observation count, which slightly muddies the scaling story given the paper's own argument that BOMO and HDBO are distinct.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned problem (BOMO): the paper convincingly argues that GP hyperparameter fitting is the bottleneck when N is large, and targets proposal-time scaling directly.

Strong empirical evaluation: five simulators plus LASSO-DNA (D=180), both natural and frozen noise protocols with well-designed passive evaluation methodology, 30 repeats with standard errors, up to N=50,000 observations, and single-core wall-clock timing that makes comparisons fair and interpretable.

Consistent, large speedups (8.5x to 151x) over TuRBO with largely comparable solution quality, plus an appropriate ablation (turbo-zero, turbo-one-nds, turbo-one-ucb) that partially disentangles the effect of the surrogate from the acquisition change.

Honest, substantive limitations section (no regret bounds, fixed K, Euclidean distance issues in high D, unsupported constraints/mixed variables) and good reproducibility (pip-installable ennbo package, ablations on K and P).

A non-trivial theory appendix: Theorem 1 verifies the PBO surrogate conditions with complete proofs, Theorem 2 gives a weighted-kNN bias-variance bound and minimax-style local rate, and Theorem 3 handles fitted variance-scale parameters via stability transfer.
The noise-free, fitting-free NDS variant is a sensible and well-justified design decision.
weaknesses: Limited originality: ENN is essentially an inverse-distance-weighted kNN estimator with epistemic variance set to c_e * d^2. This is close to Nadaraya-Watson / weighted-kNN ideas and to local GP approximations (Gramacy & Apley, Vecchia) that the authors themselves discuss; the conceptual contribution is a simplification rather than a new mechanism.

The uncertainty quantification is heuristic and weakly calibrated: held-out log-likelihood only ranks 'near the median' among surrogates (Figure 17), and the claim that 'none of the alternative surrogates... supports principled uncertainty quantification' is overstated (random forests in SMAC and DNGO provide uncertainty estimates of a sort). The independence assumption across neighbors is acknowledged but the resulting σ(x) saturates at distance-to-nearest-neighbor, which understates uncertainty in unexplored regions.

Attribution of gains is muddled: much of the speedup comes from the acquisition change (UCB/NDS instead of Thompson sampling) and from skipping hyperparameter fitting, not only from the surrogate; the ablations show turbo-one-nds and turbo-one-ucb perform comparably to turbo-one, so it remains unclear how much of the quality preservation is due to ENN versus TuRBO's trust-region machinery being robust to acquisition changes.

The convergence guarantee via PBO (Chen & Lam, 2025) is weak relative to the empirical claims: no regret bounds, and the practical acquisition (UCB with β=1, NDS sampling) differs from the scalarization analyzed in Proposition 1, leaving a gap between theory and the algorithm actually run.

Incumbent selection in the noisy variant considers only the top-K observations by y_i, a heuristic that could systematically miss good designs whose single noisy evaluation was unlucky; this choice is not ablated.

Minor presentation issues: Figure 1 shows turbo-enn nearly flat in N while the text claims O(N) scaling; several synthetic-function quality claims are only supported in the appendix; some tables (e.g., LogLik values in Tables 2-5) show large variance that complicates interpretation.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and increasingly relevant problem (BO with many observations, 'BOMO'), where surrogate fitting/proposal time dominates cheap parallel evaluations, and the motivation is clearly distinguished from high-dimensional BO.

The proposed ENN surrogate is simple, well-specified (four explicit defining properties, precision-weighted combination of K nearest neighbors), and scales linearly in N for both fitting and acquisition; the fitting-free noise-free variant (non-dominated sort over µ and σ) is a sensible further simplification.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for an engineering-flavored contribution: five problems (four Gymnasium simulators plus LASSO-DNA), both natural and frozen noise, 30 repetitions, a surrogate-free ablation (turbo-zero), acquisition ablations (turbo-one-nds, turbo-one-ucb), sensitivity studies over K and P (Appendix A), pure fitting benchmarks against Exact GP, SVGP, DNGO, SMAC, and Vecchia (Appendix B), and single-CPU wall-clock accounting.

Appendix C provides a genuine theoretical contribution: proofs of ENN surrogate properties (local consistency, sequential no-empty-ball), a weighted-kNN bias–variance bound with an n^{-2/(q+2)} local rate, a stability/transfer result for the fitted variance-scale parameters, and verification of the Chen–Lam PBO improvement conditions, yielding a convergence guarantee for the full algorithm.

The method is released as a pip-installable, open-source package (ennbo), and the limitations/future-work section is candid (fixed K, no ARD, no joint sampling, no regret bounds, Euclidean distance degradation in high D).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The core surrogate is essentially inverse-distance-squared weighted kNN regression combined with TuRBO's existing trust region and RAASP sampling machinery; the abstract's claim of 'principled uncertainty quantification' rests on an independence assumption between observations that is explicitly acknowledged as false ('we treat the estimates as independent for tractability'), and distance-proportional epistemic variance (σ_e² = c_e d²) is a heuristic, not a calibrated probabilistic model. The related-work claim that no alternative surrogate except ENN 'supports principled uncertainty quantification' is overstated (e.g., SMAC's forest-based variance estimates, DNGO's MC-dropout uncertainty).

The central empirical claim — comparable solution quality at 1–2 orders of magnitude faster proposal time — is largely predictable from the algorithm's design: removing GP hyperparameter fitting (the stated bottleneck) with a fitting-free kNN estimator will obviously be much faster. The more informative question, whether ENN's crude uncertainty degrades sample efficiency relative to GP-based methods, is answered only on a small, mostly physics-simulation benchmark suite, where many methods (including turbo-zero and random search in frozen-noise settings) reach similar near-plateau performance, limiting the discriminating power of the experiments.

The 'BOMO' setting and Figure 1 framing somewhat stacks the comparison: the baseline GP methods (ucb, turbo-one) are evaluated in a regime (N up to 50k) where exact/sparse GPs are known to be unsuitable, while stronger scalable-BO baselines that the paper itself cites (Vecchia-based optimization in Jimenez & Katzfuss 2022, which is the closest competitor) receive only brief discussion and one timing comparison rather than full optimization-quality benchmarking on the simulators.

Several methodological choices are under-justified and potentially fragile: K=10 fixed globally for all problems and dimensions; β=1 for UCB with uncalibrated σ; a single-isotropic-lengthscale analog via Euclidean distance with no ARD, which the authors themselves note will degrade as D grows — yet the headline experiments include D=180 (LASSO-DNA), where distance concentration makes the surrogate essentially uninformative and the results may reflect trust-region sampling (turbo-zero performs comparably there, at 40s vs 88s).

The convergence guarantee inherits only the relatively weak PBO framework conditions and comes with no regret bounds (acknowledged), so the theoretical contribution, while carefully executed, does not materially differentiate the method from simpler heuristics; additionally, the theoretical analysis (Appendix C) largely covers the exact-observation and fixed-(s0, ce) settings, whereas the practical noisy variant subsamples the pseudolikelihood and refits every iteration.

Reproducibility is good in spirit (open source) but incomplete in detail: the BipedalWalker controller was 'designed interactively with Cursor, GPT-5.2, and Claude Opus 4.5' and code is only at <ANONYMOUS>, the passive-evaluation protocol (num_denoise_passive seeds) introduces evaluation noise into the headline ybest comparisons, and key hyperparameters of baselines (e.g., BoTorch UCB settings, trust region parameters inherited from TuRBO) are not fully specified in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (BOMO), clearly distinguishing it from high-dimensional BO and justifying why GP surrogates become the bottleneck at large N.

The ENN surrogate is simple, well-specified (precision-weighted kNN with epistemic/aleatoric variance decomposition), and the complexity analysis is transparent and plausible; the subsampled LOO pseudolikelihood trick to keep hyperparameter fitting linear in N is a nice engineering touch with a reasonable justification.

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: five simulators/HPO tasks, both natural and frozen noise protocols (with a careful and well-argued evaluation methodology, e.g., passive evaluation seeds), 30 repetitions with standard errors, up to N=50,000, an ablation (turbo-zero), acquisition-method ablations (turbo-one-nds, turbo-one-ucb), and pure fitting benchmarks against many surrogates (exact GP, SVGP variants, DNGO, SMAC, Vecchia) under a common single-CPU protocol.

The proposal-time speedups are well supported by Table 1 and Figure 1 (roughly 9x-151x vs. turbo-one), and the pure fitting experiments isolate surrogate cost from acquisition cost, strengthening the causal story.

Appendix C provides genuine theoretical content: PBO condition verification (Theorem 1, Proposition 1), a bias-variance bound and local consistency rate for the weighted-kNN estimator (Theorem 2), and transfer to fitted variance-scale parameters (Theorem 3), with complete proofs.
Strong reproducibility: pip-installable open-source package, fixed hyperparameters (K=10), documented experimental settings, and sensitivity ablations on K and P.
Limitations section is honest and substantive (constant K, no joint sampling/Thompson sampling, Euclidean distance degradation in high D, no regret bounds, constraints/mixed variables unhandled).
weaknesses: Originality is modest: the surrogate is essentially a precision-weighted kNN regression, and nearest-neighbor conditioning already exists in Vecchia/local GP BO methods (which the authors compare to and credit). The novelty rests mainly on the extreme simplification and the fitting-free NDS variant rather than a new modeling insight.

The central claim that solution quality is 'comparable' to TuRBO is only partially supported. In some natural-noise runs (e.g., Hopper-v5, Figure 4), turbo-enn visibly lags turbo-one, and the paper does not report statistical significance tests on the quality comparisons, only mean +/- two standard errors; 'matching' quality is asserted more than demonstrated.

The UCB parameter beta=1 is fixed without justification; since ENN's sigma is not calibrated like a GP posterior and is in different units than mu, the choice of beta plausibly matters, and no sensitivity analysis over beta is provided.

The theoretical guarantees have limited bite: the noise-free analysis assumes exact observations, whereas the practical algorithm uses fitted hyperparameters and noisy data (handled only via the transfer/stability condition of Theorem 3), and there are no regret bounds; the PBO verification is for an auxiliary scalarization rather than exactly the deployed NDS/UCB procedures.

The ENN epistemic variance (ce * d^2 to neighbors) is a crude surrogate for uncertainty; a single global ce and scalar s0 (no ARD) may limit performance on problems with anisotropic structure, and the fitting-free variant sets ce=1, which is arbitrary when objective scales vary.

Comparisons to some strong scalable baselines are incomplete: parametric surrogates (DNGO/SMAC) are excluded from BO experiments citing fitting complexity, even though they are included in fitting benchmarks and would have O(N)-ish proposal times in BO.

Presentation has minor issues: the non-dominated-sort comparison between mu and sigma in the noise-free variant is somewhat ad hoc, and the heterogeneous x-axis scales (N up to 10,000 natural vs. 50,000 frozen) make visual quality comparisons across subplots difficult.
